name: Naphazoline eye drops

card.summary: Over-the-counter eye drops containing the vasoconstrictor naphazoline, which narrows swollen surface blood vessels so red eyes look whiter.
card.note: Prolonged use is not advised without identifying the cause of redness; side effects include rebound redness and raised eye pressure.

quick.overview:
Naphazoline is a decongestant that constricts blood vessels. In eye drops it narrows the swollen vessels on the white of the eye, which makes red eyes look whiter and brighter within minutes, an effect people use for a fresher, more rested face.

It has been patented since 1934 and in medical use since 1942, and is sold over the counter in products such as Clear Eyes and Naphcon-A.
quick.how: Drops are used as labelled for temporary redness, typically right before an event or photos. Labels advise against continuous use and recommend identifying the underlying cause of persistent redness.
quick.risks: Reported effects include stinging, blurred vision, dilated pupils, tearing and raised intraocular pressure; rebound redness is described with overuse. Warnings cover infants and children, and caution in severe cardiovascular disease or diabetes. Nasal use for prolonged periods is associated with rebound congestion.

lead: Naphazoline is a sympathomimetic vasoconstrictor that acts on alpha-adrenergic receptors. In eye drops it relieves red eye by narrowing swollen conjunctival blood vessels.[1] People use it to make the whites of the eyes look clearer and the eye area look less tired.

It was patented in 1934 and has been in medical use since 1942; brand names include Clear Eyes, Naphcon-A and Rohto products, and it is generally sold over the counter.[1] Wikipedia notes that temporary redness can be treated once the cause is known, but continuous use without identifying an underlying cause is not advised.[1]

Related research includes a multicentre open trial of topical naphazoline in 60 myasthenia gravis patients with drooping eyelids,[2] and reviews of imidazoline decongestants and of rebound congestion with topical nasal decongestants.[3][4]

chain: Drop applied to the eye surface
angle.text: By constricting surface vessels, naphazoline reduces redness in the white of the eye for a limited time, which changes how rested and clear the eyes look.

paras: Users reach for redness-relief drops to make eyes look clearer. The effect arises from vessel narrowing rather than a change to the cause of the redness.[1]

Naphazoline is added to eye drops for red eye and also used as a nasal decongestant.[1] In a multicentre open trial, 60 myasthenia gravis patients with blepharoptosis used topical naphazoline to test its effect on drooping eyelids.[2]

Listed eye effects include stinging, irritation, increased redness, blurred vision, dilated pupils, tearing and raised intraocular pressure.[1] Systemic warnings cover central nervous system depression in infants and children, caution in severe cardiovascular disease or diabetes, and a suggested link to stroke.[1]
Prolonged nasal use can cause rhinitis medicamentosa, rebound nasal congestion, which a 2026 review examines.[3]

Naphazoline is a mixed alpha-1 and alpha-2 adrenergic agonist; stimulating alpha receptors in conjunctival arterioles narrows them and reduces congestion.[1] A 2025 review covers imidazoline decongestants as a class.[4]
Published trials of naphazoline address varied uses, including a 2011 multicentre open trial in myasthenic blepharoptosis and a 1980 randomised comparison of ocular decongestants.[2][5]
